inline.s: This passage of sutra is saying: body and mind (the brain) are illusory, and because sentient beings deludedly cling to body and mind as self (the mark of self), they wander through birth and death.

[The four great elements] All material forms in the world are composed of the four elements earth, water, fire, and wind; hence they are called "great" — the greatness of earth, of water, of fire, of wind. Earth has solidity as its nature, water has moisture as its nature, fire has warmth as its nature, wind has movement as its nature. [The shadowy reflections of the six sense objects] The thoughts, feelings, and emotions produced when the six faculties contact the six sense objects: these are phantom reflections cast by the six faculties as they meet the six sense objects, and so they are called the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects; they are also named the mind of clinging and discrimination, which is what people ordinarily call the brain, the mind, or the intellect. [Flowers in space] That is, flowers in the sky. "Flower" is an ancient variant of "blossom."
Always remind yourself:
I am not this body, nor am I this brain
(the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects)

Whenever things go your way or against you, and whenever something circles in your mind and will not leave, you must see through each one of them, see its nature clearly, and not be deceived or entangled by it, not driven by desire, not manipulated by the brain
(the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects)

. The more thoroughly you see through them, the less you suffer and the more free you are. For all suffering comes from ignorance: from taking body and mind to be self, and from taking marks that are wholly illusory to be real — exactly like the terror of being chased by a tiger in a dream.
The
Contemplation of the True Mark of All Dharmas
translated by Master Kumarajiva, Master Hanshan's instruction on life being like a dream (see in full the essay
Life Is a Dream
) and
Master Lianchi's One Stroke to Cross Them Out (see in full the essay
One Stroke to Cross Them Out (with annotations)
) are all models of the dream-illusion contemplation. Read them earnestly and take them to heart,
and at all times verify their principle and apply it in your own life.
In the way you look at all things and events, be compassionate, forgiving, surrendered, and detached.

[Surrender] It means having no resistance in the mind toward events as they are. Having no resistance does not necessarily mean doing nothing at all; it means that no action arises out of habitual reaction. Think it over: which is more effective — action taken in a mood of resentment, or action taken calmly and objectively? Moreover, resistance to events is the root of suffering: the negative emotions and excessive actions it produces usually harm body and mind, career, and human relationships far more than the events themselves do. (See
Case Study: Moving Beyond Suffering
Mr. Jiang Weinong says in his Explication of the Diamond Sutra:
"This unwise one
(a humble way of saying "I")

has studied the Buddha's teaching for twenty years, during which, though I practiced various methods and did various contemplations, I made no progress at all. Then one day, at these four lines of verse
("All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew or a flash of lightning; thus should they be contemplated")
I suddenly seemed to awaken, and I practiced contemplation accordingly. At first it was as if near and as if far, as if clear and as if dim; it did not hold together and was not very effective.
Then I understood that I ought to exert my mind to the utmost in contemplating every circumstance and condition.
However small the matter, and whether the time was most agreeable or most disagreeable, I always sealed it with the principle that all is like a dream and an illusion
— sealed it so

, and likewise sealed the practice of the Buddha's teaching itself with the principle that all is like a dream and an illusion, never departing from this whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down. After long practice in this way, though my skill in "not grasping at marks
(wisdom)
" and "abiding in stillness
(concentration)

" is still shallow, it truly began with doing this contemplation. This mind gradually felt empty and void, and toward all circumstances and marks it gradually became unmoved within. When reading sutras my eyes felt a little brighter, and when reciting the Buddha's name I felt a little more grounded. Now I ask you all to try it; you will surely find it useful. You should know that for an ordinary being of this lowly station, who wishes to turn the light around and shine it back, apart from this there is no place to begin the work. Take care! Take care!"

The core of the dream-illusion contemplation is detachment from marks: all marks are illusory; not grasping at marks, one abides in stillness. The deluded cling to marks; the awakened are free of marks.

[Clinging to marks] Taking marks as real and so loving and hating, grasping and rejecting. [Freedom from marks] Realizing that all marks are illusory and so being without love and hate, grasping and rejecting. The Diamond Sutra says:
"All that has marks is illusory. If you see all marks as no marks
(if you see that all marks are not real)
, you see the Tathagata
(that is, you see the Buddha of your own nature)
(For annotations see in full
A Precise Explanation of the Diamond Sutra

blocks.text: 2. When a Thought Arises, Be Aware of It; Being Aware, It Is Gone

inline.s: Master Guifeng says:
"All dharmas are like dreams — the sages all say so
(all the sages say this)
. Therefore deluded thoughts are originally still, and the dust of sense objects is originally empty
(like a dream, an illusion)

. This mind of emptiness and stillness, its numinous knowing is not obscured. Just this knowing of emptiness and stillness is your true nature. Whether deluded or awakened, the mind knows of itself; it does not arise through conditions, nor does it arise because of objects. The word "knowing"
(this "knowing" of the knowing of emptiness and stillness)
is the gate of all wonders
(is the gate of all wonders)

. Because of beginningless delusion, one falsely clings to body and mind as self and gives rise to thoughts of greed and hatred. If one meets a good friend who reveals it, one may suddenly awaken to this knowing of emptiness and stillness. This knowing has no thought and no form — who then is the mark of self or the mark of person?
Awaken to all marks as empty, and the mind of itself is without thought. When a thought arises, be aware of it; being aware, it is gone. The wondrous gate of practice lies in this alone.
Therefore, though one cultivates the ten thousand practices in full,
one takes only no-thought as the foundation
. Once one attains the knowing and seeing of no-thought, then liking and disliking
(fondness and aversion)

naturally grow faint, compassion and wisdom naturally increase and brighten, karmic offenses naturally cease, and one's practice and virtue naturally advance. Having understood that all marks are no marks, one naturally arrives at the practice of no-practice. When afflictions are exhausted, birth and death are cut off. When arising and ceasing cease, still illumination appears, functioning without end — this is called Buddha."
(from the Preface to the Collected Interpretations of Chan Sources)
